name: Deep Violet
lede: Deep violet is a descriptive name used loosely for dark purples, and the books show it covers a wide stretch from blue-violet to red-purple.

sections.title: A loose phrase
sections.body: The books use "deep violet" for quite different things. A dictionary of colour defines the pansy as a deep violet or purple, and crème de violette as a deep violet [1][2]. In smalt, the blue glass pigment, the best grade was a deep violet-blue and the cheapest a pale powder blue [3]. Cobalt phosphate in its tetrahydrate form is listed as a deep violet pigment [4]. Painters see it outdoors too: on a very clear day, cloud shadows on hills three miles off can be a deep violet [5].

sections.title: In color theory and light
sections.body: Albers points out that bricks range from pale beige through orange and ochre to brown and even a deep violet, so one named object holds many colors [6]. Birren says a pale orange buff looks better with a deep violet than a lavender looks with brown [7]. A CD in daylight shows a spectrum that begins at deep violet and passes through blues and greens to the deepest red [8]. A conductor once told an orchestra to play bluer, or in a deep violet, as an example of synesthesia [9].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch comes from the xkcd color survey of 2010 [10]. It is a very dark, reddish purple: the ISCC-NBS 1955 system calls it "very deep reddish purple", under 1 unit away [10]. That is redder and darker than the blue-violet end of the spectrum the books describe [8][10]. Neighbors are [[violet]], [[purple]], [[plum]] and [[indigo]] [10].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The ColorHub archive gives a lightness of about 16 out of 100 and a chroma of 44 [10]. Contrast against white is 14.97 to 1, so white text on this color is easy to read [10].

disambiguation.gloss: the spectral violet is bluer and brighter than this swatch
